title: Motion
scope: For your school’s Grade 8 exams on the IGCSE pathway, match these motion objectives to your teacher’s topic list. These original practice questions use illustrative values, so you can concentrate on the physics.

objectives.label: Describe motion in a stated frame; distinguish distance from displacement.
objectives.note: Practise identifying the observer, path length and start-to-finish change in position.

objectives.label: Calculate average speed and distinguish speed from velocity.
objectives.note: Use total distance and total elapsed time; include direction when giving velocity.

objectives.label: Convert units and rearrange the speed equation.
objectives.note: Practise metres, kilometres, seconds, minutes and hours. Keep quantities in compatible units.

objectives.label: Read and draw distance–time and position–time graphs.
objectives.note: Read both axes before using a gradient. A distance-travelled graph cannot slope down.

objectives.label: Explain and calculate changes in velocity.
objectives.note: Include changes of direction and distinguish negative acceleration from slowing down.

objectives.label: Interpret speed–time graphs and calculate distance from their area.
objectives.note: For straight-line motion without reversing direction, a straight sloping speed–time segment means constant acceleration. Area under a speed–time graph gives distance; signed velocity–time area gives displacement.

objectives.label: Plan motion measurements and evaluate data.
objectives.note: Practise measurements, variables, repeats, fair comparisons and evidence-based conclusions.

objectives.label: Explain velocity and acceleration during free fall.
objectives.note: Use the stated value of g and state when air resistance is ignored. Check whether your school includes numerical questions on this topic.

cards.definition: The viewpoint and coordinate system used to describe position and motion.
cards.explanation: A parcel can keep its place on a walkway while its position relative to the floor changes. Both descriptions need their frame.
cards.example: A seated passenger is at rest relative to her bus and moving relative to a roadside tree.
cards.confusion: Moving relative to one frame does not mean moving relative to every frame.
cards.question: Can a parcel be at rest and moving in the same event?
cards.answer: Yes, relative to different frames: at rest on its walkway, moving relative to the floor.

cards.definition: Distance is path length. Displacement is the change in position, including direction.
cards.explanation: Follow the whole route for distance; compare just the start and finish for displacement.
cards.example: Walking 10 m east and 10 m west gives 20 m distance and zero displacement.
cards.confusion: A zero displacement does not mean no journey took place.
cards.question: After a complete lap, which can be zero: distance or displacement?
cards.answer: Displacement is zero. Distance is the lap length.
cards.cue: Distance: the route. Displacement: start to finish.

cards.definition: Total distance travelled divided by total elapsed time.
cards.explanation: Average speed spreads the whole route over the whole duration, including stops when the question includes them.
cards.example: A 100 m journey in 20 s has average speed 5 m/s.
cards.confusion: Do not divide displacement by time when asked for average speed.
cards.question: A 30 m journey takes 10 s. What is the average speed?
cards.formula: average speed = total distance ÷ total elapsed time

cards.definition: The rate of change of position, including direction.
cards.explanation: Average velocity uses displacement divided by elapsed time; instantaneous velocity describes the motion at one instant.
cards.example: 4 m/s east and 4 m/s west have the same speed and different velocities.
cards.confusion: Changing direction changes velocity even if the speed stays the same.
cards.question: A runner turns a corner at steady speed. Is velocity constant?
cards.answer: No. The direction changes, so the velocity changes.

cards.definition: Units that match the equation and the requested answer.
cards.explanation: To get m/s from distance divided by time, use metres and seconds.
cards.confusion: A number without its unit may describe the wrong quantity.
cards.question: How do you convert 90 cm to metres and 2 min to seconds?
cards.cue: Metres and seconds before metres per second.

cards.definition: Change in the vertical-axis quantity divided by change in the horizontal-axis quantity.
cards.explanation: Read the axes first. Distance-travelled–time gradient gives speed; position–time gradient gives velocity.
cards.example: Position rises uniformly by 12 m in 4 s: velocity is +3 m/s in the positive direction.
cards.confusion: A graph is not a drawing of the path; a flat position line means stationary.
cards.question: What does a negative gradient on a position–time graph mean?
cards.answer: Velocity is in the negative direction. It does not by itself say whether speed is increasing or decreasing.
cards.formula: gradient = change up the axis ÷ change along the axis
cards.cue: Read axes, then rise over run.

cards.explanation: It describes how quickly velocity changes in size or direction. Average acceleration uses the velocity change over the whole interval.
cards.example: Velocity changes from 1 m/s to 7 m/s in 3 s: average acceleration is 2 m/s².
cards.confusion: Negative acceleration means the negative direction; whether speed decreases depends on the velocity direction.
cards.question: Can something accelerate while travelling at constant speed?
cards.answer: Yes. Turning at constant speed changes the direction of velocity.
cards.formula: average acceleration = (final velocity − initial velocity) ÷ elapsed time
cards.cue: Change first, then divide by time.

cards.definition: The distance travelled during the time interval.
cards.explanation: A thin strip means speed multiplied by a short time. Adding the strips gives distance.
cards.example: A constant 3 m/s for 4 s gives rectangle area 12 m.
cards.confusion: Area under a signed velocity–time graph gives displacement; speed–time area gives distance.
cards.question: A straight line rises from 0 to 4 m/s in 3 s. What distance is covered?
cards.answer: The triangular area is ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 m.
cards.formula: distance = area under the speed–time graph

cards.definition: Repeated measurements reveal variation; a fair comparison controls relevant variables.
cards.explanation: Repeat the same procedure, compare the readings and calculate a mean where appropriate. Change one intended variable at a time.
cards.example: When varying ramp height, keep the car, timed distance, surface and release method the same.
cards.confusion: A mean can reduce random variation but cannot fix every systematic error.
cards.question: Does repeating a measurement fix a distance marked incorrectly every time?
cards.answer: No. Check and correct the distance measurement; repeating a shared systematic error does not remove it.

cards.definition: Motion under gravity alone, with other forces negligible.
cards.explanation: A ball can be in free fall while rising after release, at the highest point, and while falling.
cards.example: Ignoring air, a ball has downward acceleration about 9.8 m/s² even when its velocity is zero at the top.
cards.confusion: Zero velocity at an instant is different from zero acceleration.
cards.question: At the top of a vertical throw, which is zero: velocity or acceleration?
cards.answer: Velocity is zero. Acceleration remains downward because gravity still acts.
cards.formula: near Earth, g ≈ 9.8 m/s²; use the value stated in the question

techniques.meaning: Give the requested fact, name or value directly.
techniques.example: State the SI unit of speed: m/s.

techniques.meaning: Say what happens or what a pattern shows. Use the graph or data when provided.
techniques.example: The distance rises at a constant rate, stays constant, then rises again.

techniques.meaning: Connect the observation to a scientific reason.
techniques.example: The runner accelerates because turning changes the direction of her velocity.

techniques.meaning: Choose a suitable relationship, show substitutions, and give the result with its unit.
Refer to both cases and give a relevant similarity or difference.
techniques.example: Both boats move at 2.0 m/s, so their speeds are equal.

techniques.meaning: Offer a scientifically plausible idea suited to the evidence or situation.
techniques.example: Time crossings from video frames to reduce uncertainty about the start and finish.

techniques.meaning: Produce the requested diagram or graph with the stated labels, units and conventions.
techniques.example: Put time on the horizontal axis, label both axes with units, use uniform scales and plot the readings.

techniques.meaning: Check compatible units, the size of the result and whether it answers the quantity requested.
techniques.example: At 5 m/s, 1200 m should take 240 s; that agrees with the given journey.

techniques.meaning: Read what the question asks and supply the needed distinct points. A mark count is a guide, not a rule that every sentence earns a mark.
techniques.example: For a comparison, mention both cases. For a calculation, show your method as well as the final number.

techniques.meaning: Read the whole task, work steadily, and leave time to check units, signs, diagrams and unanswered parts.
techniques.example: If stuck, write useful known quantities, move to another question and return when you can. Use the paper’s actual instructions.

questions.title: A journey and its endpoints
questions.prompt: State the difference between distance travelled and displacement.
points: Distance is the total length of the path travelled.
Displacement is the change from the starting position to the final position, including direction.
model: Distance follows the whole route. Displacement describes where you finish relative to where you started.
accepted: Accept “length of the route” for distance and “final position minus initial position, with direction” for displacement.
questions.common: A long journey can end at its starting point, giving zero displacement.
hints: Compare the whole path with the start and finish.

questions.title: How fast, and which way?
questions.prompt: State the equation for average speed and give its SI unit.
points: Average speed = total distance travelled ÷ total elapsed time.
The SI unit is metres per second, m/s.
model: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, in m/s when distance is in metres and time in seconds.
accepted: Accept v = d/t when the symbols are identified as average speed, total distance and total elapsed time. Accept m s⁻¹ for m/s.
questions.common: Speed is not distance multiplied by time. A velocity also needs a direction.
hints: Ask how many metres are covered in each second.

questions.title: A change each second
questions.prompt: State what acceleration measures and give its SI unit.
points: Acceleration measures the rate of change of velocity.
model: Acceleration tells you how much the velocity changes each second. Its unit is m/s².
accepted: Accept “change in velocity per unit time” and m s⁻². “Change in speed per second” alone does not cover changing direction.
questions.common: Acceleration includes a change in direction, even when speed stays constant.
hints: Velocity includes direction.

questions.title: A flat line
questions.prompt: A distance-travelled–time graph is horizontal for four seconds. Explain what the object is doing during those four seconds.
points: The distance travelled does not increase during the interval.
The object is stationary during those four seconds.
model: No extra distance is covered, so its speed is zero and the object is stationary.
accepted: Accept “at rest” or “not moving”; the explanation must refer to unchanged distance during the interval.
questions.common: A horizontal line on this graph does not mean constant nonzero speed. Check the vertical axis.
hints: What happens to the distance as time passes?

questions.title: Worked example: a cycle ride
questions.prompt: A cyclist covers 1.2 km in 4.0 min. Calculate her average speed in m/s. These are illustrative values.
points: Convert 1.2 km to 1200 m and 4.0 min to 240 s.
model: Average speed = 1200 ÷ 240 = 5.0 m/s.
At 5 m/s, covering 1200 m would take 240 s, so the result is consistent.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 5 m/s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Dividing 1.2 by 4 gives km/min, not m/s.
hints: Convert both quantities before dividing.

questions.title: Your turn: find the time
questions.prompt: A runner covers 600 m at an average speed of 3.0 m/s. Calculate the time in seconds.
points: Rearrange speed = distance ÷ time to time = distance ÷ speed.
model: Time = distance ÷ average speed.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 200 s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Multiplying distance by speed does not give a time.
hints: Write speed = distance ÷ time, then isolate time.

questions.title: Worked example: gaining speed
questions.prompt: A toy vehicle moving in a straight line increases its velocity from 2.0 m/s to 10.0 m/s in 4.0 s. Calculate its average acceleration in m/s².
points: Calculate the change in velocity: 10.0 − 2.0 = 8.0 m/s.
model: Average acceleration = (final velocity − initial velocity) ÷ time.
The velocity changes by an average of 2 m/s each second.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 2 m/s² in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Using final velocity alone gives the wrong change.
hints: Find the change before finding the rate.

questions.title: Your turn: a slowing scooter
questions.prompt: A scooter moving east slows from 12.0 m/s to 4.0 m/s in 4.0 s. Take east as positive. Calculate its average acceleration in m/s².
points: Use final minus initial velocity: 4.0 − 12.0 = −8.0 m/s.
model: The negative sign means the acceleration points west, opposite to the eastward velocity in this case.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for -2 m/s² in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: A minus sign gives direction; here it also corresponds to slowing because the velocity is positive.
hints: Write both velocities with their signs.
questions.scaffold: Change in velocity = ____ − ____ = ____ m/s. Average acceleration = ____ ÷ 4.0.

questions.title: Worked example: distance under a graph
questions.prompt: A trolley starts from rest. Its speed increases uniformly to 6.0 m/s in 4.0 s, as shown. Calculate its distance travelled in those four seconds, in metres.
points: Identify the triangular area under the speed–time graph.
model: Distance is the area under the speed–time graph.
The area is a triangle: ½ × base × height = ½ × 4.0 × 6.0 = 12 m.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 12 m in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Using 6 × 4 assumes the trolley was at its final speed for the whole interval.
hints: Find the shape between the line and the time axis.

graph.caption: Illustrative trolley motion: speed increases uniformly from 0 to 6 m/s in 4 s.

questions.title: Your turn: two parts of a journey
questions.prompt: The graph shows a cart at 3.0 m/s for 4.0 s, then slowing uniformly to rest over the next 2.0 s. Calculate the total distance travelled in metres.
points: Add the areas to obtain 15 m.
model: Distance = rectangle area + triangle area.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 15 m in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: The final two seconds begin at t = 4 s, so their width is 2 s rather than 6 s.
hints: Split the area at t = 4 s.

graph.caption: Illustrative cart motion: steady speed followed by uniform slowing.

questions.title: Worked example: walking inside a carriage
questions.prompt: In a model, a carriage moves east at 8.0 m/s relative to the ground. A passenger walks east at 1.0 m/s relative to the carriage. Calculate the passenger’s speed relative to the ground in m/s.
points: Recognise that both velocities point east.
model: In one second the carriage moves 8 m east, and the passenger moves another 1 m east inside it.
Relative to the ground she moves 9 m east in that second: 9.0 m/s.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 9 m/s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: The 1 m/s and 8 m/s refer to different frames. State the frame when describing motion.
hints: Imagine where the passenger ends up after one second.

questions.title: Your turn: read a gradient
questions.prompt: A walker’s position changes uniformly from 2.0 m to 10.0 m east of a marker between t = 1.0 s and t = 5.0 s. Calculate her velocity in m/s, taking east as positive.
points: Find the change in position: 10.0 − 2.0 = 8.0 m.
model: Velocity = change in position ÷ elapsed time.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 2 m/s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Use changes in both coordinates; 10 ÷ 5 would ignore the starting point.
hints: Choose two points and subtract their coordinates.
questions.scaffold: Gradient = change in position ÷ change in time = (____ − ____) ÷ (____ − ____).

questions.title: Back at the starting gate
questions.prompt: A child walks 120 m east along a straight path, then 120 m west to the starting gate. The whole trip takes 160 s. Calculate (a) total distance, (b) displacement, and (c) average speed.
points: Displacement is zero because the final position equals the starting position.
model: (a) Total distance = 240 m.
(b) Displacement = 0 m.
(c) Average speed = 1.5 m/s. The zero displacement does not make the distance or average speed zero.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: Using zero displacement in the speed equation would calculate average velocity, not average speed.
hints: Draw the outward and return paths.

questions.title: A ball crossing a mat
questions.prompt: A ball travels 150 cm across a mat in 0.50 s. Calculate its average speed in m/s. The values describe a model measurement.
model: Average speed = 1.50 ÷ 0.50 = 3.0 m/s.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 3 m/s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: One metre is 100 cm, not 1000 cm.
hints: Put the distance in metres first.

questions.title: How far does the model ferry go?
questions.prompt: A model ferry moves at a constant speed of 2.0 m/s for 1.5 min. Calculate its distance travelled in metres.
model: Distance = 2.0 × 90 = 180 m. These are illustrative model values.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 180 m in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Minutes and metres per second must be converted to compatible units.
hints: How many seconds are there in 1.5 minutes?

questions.title: Away, waiting, and back
questions.prompt: The graph shows a walker’s position east of a marker. Describe her motion during 0–4 s, 4–7 s and 7–9 s.
points: From 0 to 4 s she moves east at a constant velocity.
From 4 to 7 s she is stationary at 8 m east of the marker.
From 7 to 9 s she moves west at a constant velocity, ending 2 m east of the marker.
model: The first rising straight segment means steady eastward motion.
The horizontal segment means no change in position.
The falling straight segment means steady westward motion. She has not yet reached the marker at t = 9 s.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: This is a position graph. The decreasing position means returning west, not a negative distance travelled.
hints: Use the direction and steepness of each segment.

graph.caption: Illustrative position–time graph; east is the positive direction.

questions.title: A model train changes velocity
questions.prompt: A model train’s velocity changes from 3.0 m/s north to 9.0 m/s north in 3.0 s. Calculate its average acceleration in m/s², taking north as positive.
model: a = (9.0 − 3.0) ÷ 3.0 = +2.0 m/s², towards the north.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 2 m/s² in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: An answer in m/s is a velocity rather than an acceleration.
hints: Find how much the velocity changes in the whole interval.

questions.title: A journey made of three shapes
questions.prompt: The graph shows a robot speeding up uniformly, moving steadily, then slowing uniformly. Calculate its total distance travelled in metres.
model: Split the area under the graph at t = 2 s and t = 5 s.
Distance = 4 + 12 + 4 = 20 m.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 20 m in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: The steady section lasts 3 s, from 2 s to 5 s.
hints: Break the area into two triangles and one rectangle.

graph.caption: Illustrative robot motion; every sloping segment is straight.

questions.title: Measure a toy car’s average speed
questions.prompt: Plan how to measure a toy car’s average speed between two marks on a clear indoor floor. State what you would measure, how you would calculate the speed, and one way to reduce timing uncertainty. You only need to describe the plan.
points: Measure the distance between the marks with a ruler or tape measure.
Measure the elapsed time between the car crossing the two marks.
Calculate average speed as measured distance divided by elapsed time.
Use a suitable improvement such as timing from video frames or increasing the timed distance while keeping the route clear.
model: Read the plan with an adult before trying it. Keep the floor clear and use a small toy car; keep away from stairs and doorways.
Measure the marked distance. Time from the front of the car crossing the first mark to the same part crossing the second. Divide distance by elapsed time.
A fixed-camera video with a known frame rate lets you identify the crossings more consistently. A longer safe timed distance also reduces the effect of reaction time.
accepted: Accept light gates or another suitable way of detecting both crossings, if available. For repeated timings, say to calculate a mean; averaging reduces random variation, rather than removing every error.
questions.common: A speed measured over the whole interval is an average; it does not prove the car had that speed at every instant.
hints: Which two measured quantities does the speed equation need?

questions.title: At the highest point
questions.prompt: A small ball has been thrown vertically upwards. At its highest point, state its velocity and its acceleration. Ignore air resistance and use g = 9.8 m/s². Explain why zero velocity at that instant does not mean zero acceleration.
points: Gravity still acts and the velocity continues changing through that instant.
model: At the highest point the ball has zero velocity, but its acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downwards.
The ball is changing from upward velocity to downward velocity; gravity has not switched off.
accepted: Accept acceleration written as −9.8 m/s² if upwards is explicitly chosen as positive. A downward direction must be clear.
questions.common: Zero velocity at one instant does not imply zero acceleration.
hints: Think about the velocity just before and just after the highest point.

questions.title: A parcel on a moving walkway
questions.prompt: A parcel rests on a moving walkway that travels steadily east. A person standing on the floor says the parcel moves; a person moving beside it on the walkway says it is at rest. Explain whether their descriptions can both be correct.
points: The parcel has zero velocity relative to the walkway.
The parcel has eastward velocity relative to the floor.
Both descriptions can be correct because they use different stated reference frames.
model: The parcel keeps the same position on the walkway, so it is at rest in that frame.
Its position relative to the floor changes eastwards, so it is moving in the floor frame. Both observations describe the same event.
accepted: Accept equivalent descriptions using “relative to the floor” and “relative to the walkway”. Both frames must be distinguished.
questions.common: There is no single privileged frame that makes the other steady-motion description an illusion.
hints: Name what each person uses as the reference.

questions.title: The turn on the athletics track
questions.prompt: A runner goes around a curved section of a track at a constant speed of 4.0 m/s. Explain whether her velocity changes and whether she is accelerating.
points: Her velocity changes because its direction changes.
Acceleration is a rate of change of velocity.
She is therefore accelerating even though her speed is constant.
model: The speedometer could keep the same reading while the direction of motion changes.
Velocity includes direction. A changing velocity means acceleration.
accepted: Accept “direction changes, so velocity changes” as the reason for acceleration. A force explanation is not required here.
questions.common: Constant speed implies zero acceleration only when direction is also unchanged.
hints: Write down what velocity contains that speed does not.

questions.title: Compare two journeys
questions.prompt: Two model boats travel at steady speeds. Boat A covers 240 m in 2.0 min. Boat B moves at 7.2 km/h. Compare their speeds using a common unit and state which is faster.
model: Boat A takes 2 × 60 = 120 s, so its speed is 2.0 m/s.
Boat B travels 7200 m in 3600 s, also 2.0 m/s. Neither is faster.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: Numbers with different units cannot be compared directly.
hints: Put both speeds in metres per second.

questions.title: Turn observations into a graph
questions.prompt: The table gives illustrative measurements of distance travelled by a toy car. On paper, draw a distance-travelled–time graph. Label both axes with units, choose a sensible scale, plot the readings and join adjacent points with straight segments for this question.
points: Put time (s) on the horizontal axis and distance travelled (m) on the vertical axis.
Choose uniform scales that include 0–8 s and 0–12 m.
Plot all five supplied points correctly.
Join adjacent points with straight segments, including a horizontal segment from 4 s to 6 s.
model: Time belongs on the horizontal axis. The distance-travelled axis needs to reach at least 12 m.
Plot (0,0), (2,4), (4,8), (6,8), (8,12). Join adjacent points with a ruler.
The horizontal section from 4 to 6 s shows that the car was stationary during that interval.
accepted: Accept any uniform axis scales that make the supplied range readable and allow the points to be plotted accurately. Hand-drawn plots should be checked on paper.
questions.common: The line is a graph against time, not a picture of the car’s route across the floor.
hints: Begin by naming each axis and writing its unit.

questions.title: Negative acceleration, increasing speed
questions.prompt: Take east as positive. A cart’s velocity changes from −2.0 m/s to −6.0 m/s in 2.0 s. Calculate its average acceleration and explain whether it speeds up or slows down.
points: The speed increases from 2.0 m/s to 6.0 m/s.
It speeds up because velocity and acceleration both point west.
model: The change in velocity is −4.0 m/s, giving an average acceleration of −2.0 m/s².
The minus signs mean west. The size of the velocity increases, so the cart speeds up.
accepted: Accept “2.0 m/s² west” for −2.0 m/s². Accept “speed increases because the magnitude of velocity increases”.
questions.common: A negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down.
hints: Keep the negative signs when subtracting; compare the sizes of the two velocities.

questions.title: A different return journey
questions.prompt: A delivery robot travels 18 m north and then 6 m south in a total time of 8.0 s. Calculate its total distance, displacement and average speed.
model: The route totals 24 m, but the robot ends only 12 m north of its starting point.
Average speed uses the route length: 24 ÷ 8.0 = 3.0 m/s.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: Use path length for average speed and start-to-finish change for displacement.
hints: Draw north as positive, then trace both legs.

questions.title: A fresh speed–time graph
questions.prompt: The graph shows a trolley accelerating uniformly along a straight line from rest to 8.0 m/s in 4.0 s. Calculate (a) its acceleration and (b) its distance travelled during these four seconds.
points: Distance is the triangular area ½ × 4.0 × 8.0.
model: (a) The gradient gives acceleration: 8.0 ÷ 4.0 = 2.0 m/s².
(b) The area gives distance: ½ × 4.0 × 8.0 = 16 m.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: The gradient and the area represent different quantities and have different units.
hints: Name what the gradient means, then name what the area means.

graph.caption: Illustrative trolley motion with uniform acceleration.

questions.title: Which measurement should be improved?
questions.prompt: A learner times a toy car over a fixed 80 cm distance three times. The recorded times are 0.40 s, 0.50 s and 0.60 s. Calculate the mean time and the speed found using that mean time, in m/s. Suggest one way to reduce timing uncertainty.
points: Speed from the mean time = 0.80 ÷ 0.50 = 1.6 m/s.
Suggest a relevant improvement, such as timing from video frames or using a longer safe timed distance.
model: The mean time is 0.50 s.
80 cm is 0.80 m, so the speed calculated using the mean time is 1.6 m/s.
Video frames at a known rate can reduce uncertainty about the crossing times. A longer clear timed distance can reduce the fractional effect of reaction time.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: Repeating and averaging can reduce random variation; it does not remove every systematic measurement error.
hints: Add all three times before dividing by the number of trials.

questions.title: Rising towards a balcony
questions.prompt: A ball is already moving upwards after leaving a hand. Ignore air resistance. State the direction of its velocity, the direction of its acceleration, and how its speed changes before it reaches its highest point.
points: Its velocity points upwards while it is still rising.
Its acceleration points downwards because of gravity.
Its speed decreases because the acceleration is opposite to its velocity.
model: During the upward part of the flight, velocity is upward and acceleration is downward.
The downward acceleration reduces the upward velocity until it reaches zero at the highest point.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: The hand exerts no continuing upward force after the ball has left it.
hints: Keep the direction of motion separate from the direction of its change.

questions.title: A lift’s recorded positions
questions.prompt: A lift moves uniformly upwards from a height of 3.0 m at t = 2.0 s to a height of 15.0 m at t = 6.0 s. Calculate its velocity in m/s, taking upwards as positive.
model: Velocity is the gradient of a height–time graph.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 3 m/s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: The elapsed time is 4 s; the final clock reading is not the journey time.
hints: Use the differences between the two positions and the two times.

questions.title: Paper A · route and displacement
questions.prompt: A child walks 35 m east and then 15 m west. State her total distance travelled and her displacement.
model: Distance = 35 + 15 = 50 m.
Displacement = 35 − 15 = 20 m east.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: Displacement needs a direction.

questions.title: Paper A · average speed
questions.prompt: A model vehicle covers 540 m in 3.0 min. Calculate its average speed in m/s.
model: Average speed = 540 ÷ (3 × 60) = 3.0 m/s.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 3 m/s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Convert minutes to seconds before dividing.

questions.title: Paper A · describe a graph
questions.prompt: The graph shows distance travelled by a walker. Describe the motion in 0–3 s and 3–5 s.
points: From 0 to 3 s the walker moves at constant speed.
From 3 to 5 s the walker is stationary.
model: The rising straight segment shows steady speed. The horizontal segment shows no extra distance, so the walker stops.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: This is a distance-travelled graph; its height is not speed.

questions.title: Paper A · acceleration
questions.prompt: A cart moves in a straight line, changing velocity from 1.0 m/s to 7.0 m/s in 3.0 s. Calculate its average acceleration in m/s².
points: Divide by 3.0 s to obtain 2.0 m/s².
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 2 m/s² in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Use a change in velocity, not the final velocity alone.

questions.title: Paper A · a fair ramp test
questions.prompt: A learner wants to find how the height of a gentle ramp affects the time a toy car takes to travel a fixed distance down it. State the variable to change, the variable to measure, and one variable to keep constant.
points: Change the vertical height of the ramp.
Measure the time between the same two marks.
Keep a relevant variable constant, such as the car, ramp surface, distance between marks or release method.
model: Change ramp height and measure the time over a fixed marked distance.
Use the same car and surface and release it from rest without a push. Read the plan with an adult before trying it; keep the ramp low and the stopping area clear.
accepted: Accept “independent variable” for ramp height, “dependent variable” for time, and any relevant named control such as the same car or fixed timed distance.
questions.common: Changing the car at the same time would make the comparison unfair.

questions.title: Paper A · velocity at the top
questions.prompt: At the highest point of a vertical upward throw, a student says, “Its velocity is zero, so its acceleration is zero.” Explain the error. Ignore air resistance.
points: Zero velocity at an instant does not mean zero rate of change of velocity.
Gravity still gives the ball downward acceleration at the highest point.
model: The velocity passes through zero as it changes from upward to downward. Gravity still acts, so acceleration remains downward.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: A momentary zero value is different from an unchanging value.

questions.title: Paper B · two reference frames
questions.prompt: A passenger stays in her seat while a bus travels steadily north. State whether she is moving relative to the bus and relative to a tree beside the road.
points: She is at rest relative to the bus.
She is moving north relative to the tree.
model: Her position in the bus stays the same. Her position relative to the tree changes northwards.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: Always say what the motion is measured relative to.

questions.title: Paper B · speed with a stop
questions.prompt: A robot covers 360 m in 120 s, waits for 60 s, then covers another 360 m in 120 s. Calculate its average speed for the whole journey, including the stop, in m/s.
model: The waiting time is part of the whole journey.
Average speed = 720 ÷ 300 = 2.4 m/s.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 2.4 m/s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Leaving out the stop would overestimate the average speed for the whole journey.

questions.title: Paper B · distance from a graph
questions.prompt: A cart moves at 5.0 m/s for 4.0 s and then slows uniformly to rest over the next 4.0 s. Use the graph to calculate the total distance travelled in metres.
model: Distance = area under the speed–time graph.
Distance = 20 + 10 = 30 m.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 30 m in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: Use the width of the slowing interval, not the final clock reading.

graph.caption: Illustrative cart motion: steady speed, then uniform slowing.

questions.title: Paper B · changing direction
questions.prompt: A model car travels around a circular track at constant speed. Explain why it is accelerating.
points: Its direction of motion, and therefore its velocity, changes.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
model: Velocity includes direction. Going around the circle changes velocity, so the car is accelerating even at constant speed.
accepted: Equivalent correct scientific wording is accepted; the listed points explain what earns credit.
questions.common: A constant speed does not guarantee a constant velocity.

questions.title: Paper B · judging repeated readings
questions.prompt: A learner records times of 2.1 s, 2.0 s and 2.2 s for a toy car travelling the same marked distance. State the mean time and explain one reason to take repeated readings.
points: Repeats show variation and averaging can reduce the effect of random timing error.
model: The mean is 2.1 s.
Repeats reveal how much results vary; using a mean can reduce the effect of random timing differences.
accepted: Accept “reduce the effect of random error” or “make a mean less affected by individual timing variations”. Repeats alone do not remove systematic error.
questions.common: Repeats do not automatically remove a systematic error such as a wrongly marked distance.

questions.title: Paper B · falling faster
questions.prompt: A small ball is released from rest. Ignore air resistance and use g = 9.8 m/s². Calculate its speed after 0.50 s in m/s.
points: Use change in velocity = acceleration × time, with initial velocity zero.
model: The ball gains 9.8 m/s of downward velocity each second.
After 0.50 s its speed is 4.9 m/s; its velocity is directed downwards.
accepted: Accept equivalent numerical notation for 4.9 m/s in the requested unit. Award method points separately using the suggested marking guidance.
questions.common: The speed grows from zero; 9.8 m/s² is an acceleration, not its speed after every interval.

sources.title: IES: Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning
